subject: mathematics_2a
question_text: Prove that (C₀ + C₁)·(C₁ + C₂)·(C₂ + C₃)·…·(Cₙ₋₁ + Cₙ) = ((n + 1)ⁿ/n!)·C₁·C₂·…·Cₙ.

mark_split.label: Take Cᵣ₋₁ out of each bracket

recall_prompt: Say how you would prove this — how you take Cᵣ₋₁ out of each bracket, what 1 + Cᵣ/Cᵣ₋₁ simplifies to, what the product of all the (n + 1)/r factors is, and why C₀C₁…Cₙ₋₁ can be written as C₁C₂…Cₙ.
insider_note: Take Cᵣ₋₁ out of every bracket, not Cᵣ — the inverted ratio never simplifies. The last mark is the line C₀ = Cₙ = 1, which turns C₀C₁…Cₙ₋₁ into the C₁C₂…Cₙ the right side shows.

steps.label: Take Cᵣ₋₁ out of each bracket
steps.margin_note: First two marks. Cᵣ₋₁ + Cᵣ = Cᵣ₋₁(1 + Cᵣ/Cᵣ₋₁). Do it to every bracket and collect the C's in front.
steps.memory_tip: Take Cᵣ₋₁ out of each bracket, not Cᵣ. A RATIO of consecutive coefficients has a formula; a sum does not.

recall.must_convey: That each bracket Cᵣ₋₁ + Cᵣ is written as Cᵣ₋₁(1 + Cᵣ/Cᵣ₋₁), so the left side is C₀C₁…Cₙ₋₁ times a product of brackets (1 + Cᵣ/Cᵣ₋₁).
accept: take C r minus one out of each bracket to get one plus C r by C r minus one, and collect C nought C one up to C n minus one in front
each factor is C r minus one times one plus the ratio of consecutive coefficients
factor the first coefficient out of every bracket
prathi bracket lo C r minus one bayataki teeste one plus C r by C r minus one vasthundi
the product becomes C nought to C n minus one times brackets of one plus a ratio
heard_as: C r by C r minus one

steps.why: A sum of two consecutive coefficients has no product formula, but a RATIO of consecutive coefficients does. Factoring turns every sum into 1 + a ratio.
common_mistakes: Taking out Cᵣ instead of Cᵣ₋₁, which gives the inverted ratio.
Losing count of how many C's were taken out — there are n, from C₀ to Cₙ₋₁.

steps.label: Simplify each bracket to (n + 1)/r
steps.margin_note: Third and fourth marks. ⁿCᵣ/ⁿCᵣ₋₁ = (n − r + 1)/r, so 1 + (n − r + 1)/r = (n + 1)/r.
steps.memory_tip: ⁿCᵣ/ⁿCᵣ₋₁ = (n − r + 1)/r, so 1 + that is (n + 1)/r. The same numerator every time.

recall.must_convey: That Cᵣ/Cᵣ₋₁ = (n − r + 1)/r, so each bracket 1 + Cᵣ/Cᵣ₋₁ = (n + 1)/r.
accept: C r by C r minus one is n minus r plus one by r, add one and the bracket is n plus one by r
each bracket simplifies to n plus one over r
the ratio formula gives one plus n minus r plus one by r which is n plus one by r
ratio formula vadithe prathi bracket n plus one by r avthundi
the brackets are n plus one by one, n plus one by two, up to n plus one by n

steps.why: The r in the denominator and the −r in the numerator cancel when 1 is added, leaving the same numerator n + 1 in every bracket. That is why (n + 1)ⁿ appears.
common_mistakes: Using (n − r)/(r + 1), which is the ratio one index up.

steps.label: Multiply the n brackets
steps.margin_note: Fifth and sixth marks. n brackets each with numerator n + 1 give (n + 1)ⁿ; the denominators 1·2·…·n give n!.
steps.memory_tip: Count the brackets: exactly n of them, so (n + 1)ⁿ on top and 1·2·…·n = n! below.

recall.must_convey: That the product of the n brackets is (n + 1)ⁿ over 1·2·…·n = n!, so the left side is C₀C₁…Cₙ₋₁·(n + 1)ⁿ/n!.
accept: multiply the n brackets, n plus one to the n on top and one into two into up to n which is n factorial below
the product of the brackets is n plus one to the n over n factorial
n factors of n plus one over r give n plus one to the power n by n factorial
n brackets multiply cheste n plus one power n by n factorial vasthundi
the denominators one to n multiply to n factorial
heard_as: n plus one to the n

steps.why: Counting the brackets matters: there are exactly n, from r = 1 to r = n, which gives the power n and the factorial n!.
common_mistakes: Leaving the product 1·2·…·n unnamed instead of writing n!.

steps.label: Replace C₀ by Cₙ
steps.margin_note: Seventh mark. C₀ = Cₙ = 1, so C₀C₁…Cₙ₋₁ = C₁C₂…Cₙ. That is the only difference between the two sides.
steps.memory_tip: C₀ = Cₙ = 1, so C₀C₁…Cₙ₋₁ equals C₁C₂…Cₙ. That is the only difference between the two sides.

recall.must_convey: That C₀ = Cₙ = 1 lets C₀C₁…Cₙ₋₁ be written as C₁C₂…Cₙ, which gives the right side.
accept: C nought and C n are both one so the product C nought to C n minus one is the same as C one to C n, giving the right side
replace C nought by C n since both equal one

steps.why: The right side lists C₁ to Cₙ while the left side produced C₀ to Cₙ₋₁; since both end coefficients are 1, the two products are equal.
common_mistakes: Ending with C₀C₁…Cₙ₋₁ and not matching the right side's C₁…Cₙ.
Claiming C₀ = Cₙ without saying both are 1.
